title: Strong vs Eventual Consistency
sources: AWS, 'DynamoDB read consistency' (docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/HowItWorks.ReadConsistency.html): eventually consistent reads (the default) may not reflect a just-completed write, and consistency across all copies is usually reached within a second; strongly consistent reads return the most up-to-date data reflecting all successful writes, at higher latency and cost

Vogels, 'Eventually Consistent' (CACM 2009): if no new updates are made to an object, eventually all accesses will return the last updated value; strong consistency means after an update completes, any subsequent access returns the updated value

System Design Primer / AlgoMaster 'Strong vs Eventual Consistency': strong consistency suits banking and payments, eventual consistency suits social media likes, view counts and feeds where a short lag is acceptable in exchange for speed and availability

lines.text: You like a post, and the count goes up,
but your friend still sees the old number.
That's not a bug. It's eventual consistency.
The price just changed from ten to twelve dollars.
With strong consistency, no branch answers
until every branch has the new price.
With eventual consistency, each branch answers right away,
so for a moment, one still says ten,
but once the news arrives, they all agree.
A like counter? Eventual is fine, and much faster.
So that count isn't wrong. It's just catching up.
Tomorrow: what gets kicked out of a full cache?
